walkthroughs.body_html:
Theme B: Religion & Life — a core area of GCSE Religious Studies.

Working through it builds the schema you need: the key terms, how they connect, and how to use them together.

Theme B: Religion & Life brings together several ideas you need to use as a set, not in isolation.

Lock in the vocabulary first, then practise pulling the ideas together to answer real questions.

Use the activities in this adventure to build familiarity with Theme B: Religion & Life.

Practise vocabulary, calculations and free-text questions to lock in the learning.

mcqs.q: How does Reform Judaism differ from Orthodox Judaism?
options: Reform Judaism treats Jewish law (halakhah) as evolving and not strictly binding, embraces modernity, and grants gender equality; Orthodox Judaism holds halakhah as divinely given and binding in detail, with traditional practice maintained.
Orthodox Judaism is a different religion from Reform Judaism.
Moksha is the Hindu word for heaven.
Reform Jews don't believe in God and Orthodox Jews do.

mcqs.q: How do samsara, karma and moksha fit together in Hindu thought?
options: Orthodox Judaism is a different religion from Reform Judaism.
Samsara is the cycle of rebirth; karma is the law of action and consequence that drives rebirth; moksha is liberation from samsara — these form a connected chain, not three independent ideas.
Moksha is the Hindu word for heaven.
Samsara, karma and moksha are three separate Hindu deities.
The first five books of the Hebrew Bible (Genesis, Exodus, Leviticus, Numbers, Deuteronomy) — traditionally attributed to Moses and containing law, narrative and covenant.
The Torah is the same as the Book of Genesis.
The Torah is a single scroll containing every Jewish text.
Orthodox Judaism is a different religion from Reform Judaism.
